# 0004. Use UUIDv7 primary keys, generated by Postgres 18
Date: 2026-11-24 · Status: accepted

## Context
Every table needs an ID. IDs appear in URLs and API responses, so counting
numbers (`/profiles/42`) let anyone walk through every record and estimate how
many users and requests Vouch has. Unguessable IDs don't replace permission
checks (IDOR is prevented by checking ownership on every request), but they add
a second layer. Fully random IDs land all over a sorted index, which slows
inserts as tables grow. The same IDs must work from Python now and Java from
Phase 1.5.

## Options considered
1. Auto-increment `bigint` — small (8 bytes), fast, readable / guessable;
   leaks counts.
2. Random UUID (v4) — unguessable / 16 bytes; random index positions slow
   inserts at scale.
3. UUIDv7 — time first, then random: new IDs land near the end of the index
   like auto-increment, and can't be guessed by counting / 16 bytes; anyone
   holding an ID can read when the row was created.
4. Auto-increment inside the database plus a separate public UUID — fast joins
   and safe URLs / two IDs per row to keep straight everywhere.

For option 3, who generates the ID:
- the app (Python 3.14 has `uuid.uuid7()`) — works on Postgres 17.5 today /
  Java has no built-in v7, so the port needs a library; seed SQL can't make one.
- the database (Postgres 18 has `uuidv7()`) — one source for Python, Java and
  SQL, as a column default / means upgrading from Postgres 17.5.

## Decision
UUIDv7 for every primary key, with `DEFAULT uuidv7()` in Postgres 18. The app may
still pass its own ID when it needs to know it before inserting.

## Consequences
Easier: URLs don't reveal counts; one ID per row; Python, Java and seed scripts
all get the same kind of ID.
Harder: IDs are 16 bytes and hard to read aloud; the stack, CI and seeder move
to Postgres 18 (the official image stores data under a new path, so the
compose volume mount must change; local data is re-seedable).
Watch: index size and insert speed at 10M rows (Phase 8).
